title: Order-agnostic diffusion models for imputation
summary: A from-scratch implementation of ARDM (Hoogeboom et al., ICLR 2022), tested on images and tabular data to establish where order-agnostic generation holds up.
context: Probabilistic & Generative ML Coursework (MSc). Binarized MNIST and the UCI Mushroom dataset

sections.heading: The problem
body: Standard autoregressive models generate left to right, in a fixed order. That's bad for imputation, where missing values can sit anywhere. ARDM's fix: randomise the generation order at every training step.
list: Goal: implement the paper from scratch and identify where order-agnostic generation helps in practice, not just where the theory predicts it.

sections.heading: Approach
body: Bidirectional Transformer (~2M params, no causal mask), trained under the ARDM objective.
list: Training step: random permutation, random step, mask everything after it, loss computed at only that one position.
Experiment 1: imputation on binarized MNIST across a range of observation rates.
Experiment 2: head-to-head vs. a small CNN under the same objective.
Experiment 3: transfer test onto categorical tabular data.

sections.heading: Result
list: Imputation requires no architecture change or retraining: fix the observed pixels, sample the rest in random order.
Model uncertainty (pixel entropy, 50 completions) rises as expected: 0.037 bits at 90% visible, up to 0.219 bits at 10% visible.
Parallel block sampling: 46x faster than sequential (0.5s vs. 27.3s) for a small quality cost.

sections.heading: Transformer vs. CNN
list: The advantage appears once context is sparse: level with a small CNN at 90% and 50% visible, and clearly ahead at 10% visible.

sections.heading: Further work
list: Tabular transfer: accuracy beat random (0.40-0.56 vs. 0.04), though test loss stayed above validation loss. More data or a revised vocabulary design is the next thing to try.
